stops.title: The question
stops.text: Welcome to the second paper in the hearing group. Voxtral showed how a language model can listen. Voxtral Realtime asks a harder question: can it write down what you say while you are still saying it, and stay as accurate as a model that waits for the whole recording? The answer is a 4.4 billion parameter model that transcribes 13 languages with less than half a second of delay. For your Part A, keep one fact in mind from the start: this model hears speech and writes text, nothing more.

stops.title: One way in, one way out
stops.text: Here is the whole model on one page. Follow the gold path: speech becomes a Mel spectrogram, goes through a causal encoder, and an adapter turns every 80 milliseconds of sound into one embedding. That embedding is added to the model's own last word, and the decoder writes the next token. Now look at the grey boxes. No images, no video, no typed question, no spoken answer. So in your project this model is a component, not the whole system.

stops.title: Why not just chunk Whisper?
stops.text: Why build a new model at all? Because the usual shortcut breaks. Whisper is trained while seeing the whole sentence, future included. If you feed it audio in chunks, it must answer before the future arrives, and the lower the delay, the worse that mismatch gets. A native streaming model trains exactly the way it runs: only past audio, with the text lagging behind by a fixed delay. Notice the three needs listed at the bottom. The rest of the paper supplies each one.

stops.title: From sound to tokens
stops.text: This is the audio half of your Part A answer. Sixteen thousand samples a second become 100 Mel frames, a strided convolution halves that to 50, and the adapter stacks four encoder frames into one decoder step. So the language model takes exactly one step every 80 milliseconds. Every layer in the encoder is causal, meaning it never looks ahead, and sliding windows keep memory bounded, so the stream can run for as long as you like.

stops.title: One knob for delay
stops.text: Here is the paper's key idea. The user chooses a delay, called tau, anywhere from 80 to 2400 milliseconds. Tau becomes a small vector, and inside every decoder block it rescales the input to the feed-forward layer. Attention is left untouched. That costs about five million parameters on a 4.4 billion parameter model, yet one set of weights now serves every delay. The ablation later in the tab shows this beats simply adding the delay to the input.

stops.title: Teaching it when to speak
stops.text: How does the decoder learn when to write? Through its training targets. Every 80 millisecond frame gets exactly one token: a pad token while it waits, then a word boundary token once a word is finished and the delay has passed, then the word itself. Words that finish together share one boundary token, so the decoder still sees ordinary text. Keep this in mind: building these targets needs word timestamps, which matters if you ever fine-tune this model.

stops.title: Does it work?
stops.text: This is the headline chart. The magenta line is average word error across 13 languages as you allow more delay. At half a second it is close to offline Whisper; at about one second it beats Whisper and the leading commercial streaming service; at 2.4 seconds it gets within one point of Mistral's own offline model. The trade-off is simple and honest: every extra bit of waiting buys accuracy, and you choose where to stand.

stops.title: Not equal for everyone
stops.text: Before you celebrate, look at this chart. Average numbers hide big gaps between languages. At half a second of delay, English has about five percent error, while Arabic has twenty two and a half. On crowd recorded Common Voice, every model in the paper is above forty five percent on Arabic, so the authors drop Arabic from the averages. For you, this is a gift: a ready made fairness experiment for Part C.

stops.title: What you take from it
stops.text: So how do you use this in Assignment 1? Treat Voxtral Realtime as the ears of a pipeline. Transcribe the spoken question, then pass the transcript and the image to a small vision language model that you fine-tune with QLoRA. Pick a long delay, since your task is not live. Check memory and library support before you try to fine-tune the 4.4 billion parameter model itself. Next, LFM2 shows a different design, a compact hybrid model built for speed on small devices.
